claims.text: Heavy lifetime alcohol users have a 2- to 5-times higher risk of dying due to alcohol-related cancers compared with lifetime light users.
Men who consumed less than 5 drinks per day throughout their lifetime had a 24% lower cardiovascular disease mortality compared with lifetime light users.
Women who were moderate to occasionally heavy alcohol users had a 34-46% lower risk of death from coronary heart disease compared with light users.
The inverse association between alcohol consumption and cardiovascular disease mortality is only present among individuals who had no chronic disease at enrollment.

evidence.description: Heavy users (>5 drinks/day for men and >2.5 drinks/day for women), regardless of time of cessation, had a 2- to 5-times higher risk of dying due to alcohol-related cancers, compared with subjects with lifetime light use (≤1 and ≤0.5 drink/week for men and women, respectively).
Compared with lifetime light users, men who used <5 drinks/day throughout their lifetime had a 24% lower cardiovascular disease mortality (95% confidence interval 2-41).
The risk of death from coronary heart disease was also found to be 34-46% lower among women who were moderate to occasionally heavy alcohol users compared with light users.
However, this relationship was only evident among men and women who had no chronic disease at enrollment.

methodologies.name: Competing risks survival analysis of self-reported lifetime alcohol consumption
methodologies.description: Multivariable hazard ratios were estimated for cause-specific mortality according to lifetime alcohol consumption patterns using a competing risks model.
datasets: European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC)
conditions: Self-reported alcohol consumption at ages 20, 30, 40, or 50 years and at enrollment

limitations.text: There is limited evidence for an association between the pattern of lifetime alcohol use and cause-specific risk of death.
Potential health benefits of alcohol use are difficult to establish due to the possibility of selection bias and competing risks related to diseases occurring later in life.
